strongest_things: 08-three-futures.md — F2, the finding that the headline number is prompt text. `RecommendedRecipe.match_score` is a model-authored integer and the "Base score = (available ingredients / total required) * 100" formula at inventory_recommender.py:159-162 is instructions to Gemini, not code, while RecipeRecommendationModal.tsx:303-304 renders it as `{recipe.match_score}%` in 2xl bold. I verified both. "We are the clearest instance of the gap we describe" is a genuine, demonstrable, forty-second-on-stage finding, and it survives the demand-side collapse because it is a defect claim about our own product rather than a market claim.

08-three-futures.md — the Frozen Results paragraph device, repeated for all three options: every number is a blank with the exact query that will fill it printed beside it, and "any sentence whose query does not exist is deleted that day." This is the structural fix for fabricated results and it is the single most transferable idea in either file. Protect it.

08-three-futures.md (close third) — F5 is substantively correct and I re-verified it end to end: web/src/app/api/users/route.ts has no auth.getUser, uses supabaseServer built from SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY (supabaseServer.ts:5), selects id/fullname/email from public."User", and that table does have ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (remote_schema.sql:440) — so the service-role bypass is real rather than vacuous. Only the "executed attack" framing is wrong, not the finding.

09-pivot.md — the two prior-art self-kills. "So **do not build an RLS linter** — that is solved" (Supabase pgTAP `tests.rls_enabled`, `policies_are`) and "**We must not build a red-team framework.** Generic injection detection is done" (promptfoo). Refuting your own novelty claim before the marker does, and then naming the narrower thing that is actually unsolved (route → table → migration → policy; the rowcount oracle), is the best argumentation in either file.

09-pivot.md — the epistemic labelling. The 19th defect is marked "INFERENCE (not executed) ... treat as hypothesis until run"; `Amihua` is reported as a fifth identity whose mapping is "**unknown**, and the report should say so rather than guess"; and the verdict volunteers that "our headline IDOR was a false positive at system level — that disclosure is the credibility of the whole project." Also strong and rare: the verdict puts a go/no-go question to the instructor before any hours are spent.
result.overall:
Neither file is clean, and the damage is concentrated in their recommendations rather than their evidence sections. The repository facts in 08 (F1-F9) are good work — I spot-checked F2, F4, F5 and F3 against the tree and they hold — but the argument built on top of them does not.

Three things would hurt most if a marker found them first. (1) SAFE's line items sum to 108 h, not the "~96 h" in its own heading, which breaks the file's own "≤ 100 h" commitment and the 12-milestones 100 h capacity; BOLD (98) and WILD (88) both add up, so the only option nobody totalled is the one recommended. (2) 08 recommends the single option with zero demand-side evidence — the 851-entry Reddit sweep returned ZERO hits for eleven explainability phrasings — and demotes the two options the same corpus actively supports ("glass cleaner shows up as one in stock but in reality I have none" is BOLD's thesis; "the ones that force you to enter every single ingredient manually are the worst" is WILD's). The recommendation is inverted relative to the only user evidence the team holds, and the file has no answer because it never saw the sweep. (3) SAFE's receipt is a three-way object (item + date + points + correctable); the twice-narrowed G1 says only the four-way conjunction survives, and SAFE contains neither the nutrient constraint nor the substitution reason. So the option pitched as the differentiator ships something Grocy, Remy and RecipeFix already cover between them.

On kill signals specifically, the file opens by promising "a kill signal that is an observable condition with a number and a date." WILD's is the only one that basically works, and even it is compromised by its dataset being described two different ways (team-hand-written fixture vs. collected from ≥8 testers). SAFE's needs an oracle that is an 8 h SAFE deliverable and zero hours are allocated to the baseline run. BOLD's fires at the end of week 3 of 4, after a 98 h build is essentially paid for, and measures calibration against self-report that the adjacent Biggest-risk paragraph says is not ground truth. Every threshold — 3/100, 70/100, 50%, 80%, 20 points — is an invented number; the only base-rate data anywhere is "the two real hallucinations the pre-mortem recorded", two observations with no denominator. And there is no budget kill signal at all, despite the budget being named "the binding constraint, not the market."

One correction to the task framing: 09 does NOT recommend staying the course. Its verdict is "**Pivot — but pivot the form, not the subject ... build Project Kind 1**," which directly contradicts 08's "**Build SAFE**" from the same date and model — SAFE's plan is five new production files including a migration, and 09's whole case is that the team has zero commits behind migrations, RLS and production .ts/.tsx. Whoever reads these two files in sequence will notice. Asked the intended question anyway: 09's pivot conclusion is strengthened by the zero-demand finding, but only by accident — 09 never mentions the market, the gap, or G1-G4 at all, and its actual stated reasons are a commit histogram (counts are not hours; 81 of 99 touched files are .md from a documentation phase) and a capability constraint that its own recommended option also trips (Kind 1's executed pass "needs seed SQL, the one skill with zero commits behind it", and the demo fix is a production .ts change). So 09 reaches a defensible verdict on undefended reasoning. The fix for both files is the same and it is small: put the 851-entry zero-hit result in front of the recommendation, re-total SAFE honestly against 100 h, and let the choice be argued on measurability rather than on a market gap the team can no longer claim.

result.overall:
Both files are unusually well-evidenced at the file:line level and both are weakest exactly where they stop citing and start persuading. 10-team-fit's methodological core (§0, §2, §3) is genuinely argued; its attack on the rival and its people-risk section are not — "rehabilitating it three sections later" and "crediting us with the upstream team's TypeScript fluency" carry no quote in the one file where they are load-bearing (the supporting line exists at p1b/result/codex/README.md:162, but it is hedged with "but not which current member owns each skill" and lives in 06, not here), and §5 then commits the exact absence-to-ability inference §0 forbids by declaring a bus factor of 1. The file also asserts "testing is the one thing this team has demonstrated densely" while §5 and §7 establish that it was one person writing mostly source-text greps.

On the specific assignment question for 12: the document notes its warning and does not act on it. The 5.25 h margin is called the failure mode in the first line, the fix is named in the same sentence, and then every subsequent line of the file keeps N5b — the table still totals 94.75, line 51 still prints "Margin: 5.25 h", the classification table still plans N5b with a fallback slice. The acting happens in 14-cut-list.md (CUT 1, margin → 14.00) and 13-name-the-test.md (N4 under-costed by 6 h; N2+N3+N4+N5a "does not close"), which means the graded D3 ships a plan its own siblings have already declared infeasible. Worse, the recommended cut is the only defect the file proves has no mitigation at all, and 12 never states that cost, though 14 and 15 both do.

On the hour estimates: exactly one milestone number has a stated basis. 8.75 h derives from the per-defect triage at 03-engineering-evidence.md:132, and D6 (1.5 h) and D4 (2.0 h) from the table at :99-102. N1 12.0, N2 24.0, N3 22.0, N4 18.0, N5a 10.0, the "6 of the 22 h" split, and the entire 60 h overhead decomposition (report 24 / poster 12 / demo 10 / integration 14) have no derivation anywhere in the repository — they are vibes with a decimal point. The irony worth fixing before a marker finds it: the file calls 8.75 "the least evidenced number in this document" and cuts it, when it is the best-evidenced one; meanwhile N5a prices the same edits the triage costs at 3.5 h at 10.0 h, and that unexplained ~6.5 h is larger than the margin the whole verdict turns on. Reclaiming it from N5a rather than from the security milestone would restore the headroom without dropping the unmitigated hole.

Two staleness items need fixing before submission: 12's closing differentiation sentence is broader than what later runs left standing (the four-way conjunction), and P3's Plan to Eat quote is treated as "evidence that the problem is real" when the 851-entry Reddit sweep returned zero demand-side hits — the same shape as the Sketch-mockup screenshot.

Backed by a real capability: Hypothesis 6.141.1 is a declared dev dependency in backend/pyproject.toml and already used in backend/tests/test_recommender.py, so the property-testing claim behind F1's testability-3 is one of the few capability assertions in the file that checks out.
result.overall:
Not a clean audit. The file is real work — every repo-dependent claim I spot-checked (inventory_recommender.py 245 lines and its prose-only expired guard at :157, the transfer merge at :67, share/route.ts's anon client with no auth.getUser and no shopping_list_shares migration, the UNIQUE (user_id, ingredient_id, location) constraint, the goals route's typeof/NaN-only validation, Hypothesis in pyproject.toml) is accurate, and §0.3 and SR-EXP are genuinely strong. But the argument layer has serious problems, and they cluster in exactly the place my assignment pointed.

On the RecipeFix finding specifically: the artifact is the vendor's own App Store description plus an example recipe page on the vendor's own marketing site. That is a shipped binary plus marketing copy — it shows someone asserted the feature, not that the app does it. The document then escalates it twice: 'a real rendered rationale' (it is vendor collateral) and 'paying-customer-validated' (no rating count, review count, revenue or download figure appears anywhere, and the iTunes payload the run already fetched carries userRatingCount). It nominates that as 'the best slide you have'. This is the Cooklist/Sketch-mockup failure repeated, one bar lower — Cooklist was at least confirmed by real user reviews, RecipeFix by nothing. The same pattern governs the Use It Up finding in P20 §0.1, which is a solo developer's v1.0.8 release notes treated as proof that F1, F3 and F4 ship 'in one binary'.

On P20's scoring: the arithmetic is correct in every row (I checked all five NETs and the stated −6…+15 range), and most cells carry a real per-axis justification. Two cells are backfilled. F1 user-demand 2 is scored entirely on vendor marketing copy while F5 gets 1 for 'no user asks for this' — vendor copy is worth a full point over nobody asking, on a demand axis, in a project where an 851-entry Reddit sweep returned zero. F4 user-demand 2 is justified by the word 'real' and nothing else. More structurally: the rubric picks F5 (+10), the ruling picks F1 (+9), and the document has to argue past its own table twice ('Why F1 over F3'; 'Why F1 over F5'). The arguments are decent, but a marker will ask what the rubric was for.

The single most damaging item is budgetary, not evidential: P19 §6 prices its binding safety rules at ≈40 h and says they hold 'regardless of the DEAD verdict'; P20 §5 funds 7 h of them and prints '142.25 / 160 — 17.75 h slack'. Honour P19 and the plan is ~175 h. Add P13's competing 115 h recommendation for the feature P20 explicitly refuses, and the file contains three mutually incompatible budgets. Fix the budget contradiction and the RecipeFix/Use It Up provenance hedges first; those four edits cost an hour and remove most of the exposure.

findings.heading: CUT 7 — the live baseline, entirely / THE IRREDUCIBLE CORE (poster paragraph)
findings.quoted_sentence: `grep -c "validate\|verify\|check"` over the 245-line file returns **0**. No line of code anywhere recomputes or checks that number. We can state that as fact with a file, a line and a command a reader can re-run
findings.what_is_wrong: The command returns 0 only because grep is case-sensitive: `grep -in` returns 1 hit, and it is line 238, a comment reading `# Validate and return`, sitting directly on the `RecipeRecommendedRecipe(**rec)` call that DOES run Pydantic validation on the model's output — so the one claim that survives all ten cuts and appears verbatim in the core poster paragraph (line 180, "zero validation calls in 245 lines") is falsified by the exact command the document invites a marker to re-run.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the grep with the demonstrable and strictly stronger claim: `match_score: int  # 0-100` at :50 carries its range only in a comment, while `num_recipes: int = Field(default=5, ge=1, le=10)` at :42 on the same model enforces its bounds — so the field the user sees is the one field the schema declines to constrain, and nothing recomputes it. Cite :42 and :50 side by side and drop the word "zero validation".

findings.heading: Budget reconciliation (three lines) — vs 14's BUDGET VERDICT
findings.quoted_sentence: The full 61 h of test-build sits inside N2+N3+N4+N5a (74 h combined), leaving 13 h for implementation in those milestones — that does not close

The honest version is 14's with 13's correction applied: the core is 54.00 h of implementation PLUS the test-build for the surviving claims, which 13 prices at roughly 24 h (F0+T1+T2+T5) — so state the core as ~70 h, not 54, or state explicitly that the 54 h core figure already embeds its tests and re-derive N4a/N4b from 13's hour column.

findings.heading: T10 — The date on the receipt is the date that actually disqualifies the food
findings.quoted_sentence: Today: `item.expiration_date \|\| existingItem.expiration_date` at `transfer/route.ts:66` overwrites the stored date while `:65` sums quantities — measured, expect **4/8** (it is right only when the incoming date is NULL or already earlier)

findings.heading: T10 — The date on the receipt is the date that actually disqualifies the food
findings.quoted_sentence: The date on the receipt is the date that actually disqualifies the food
findings.what_is_wrong: `user_inventory` upserts by (user_id, ingredient_id, location) and SUMS quantities with no per-purchase lots, so no single stored date can be the date that disqualifies the food: the current rule makes the aggregate row look too fresh, and the proposed earliest-of-two fix (14's Cut 10, priced 3.5 h) makes it look too stale — the fix does not make the benefit true, it inverts the error, and neither file says so.
findings.suggested_fix: Restate the benefit as what the schema can support: "the receipt prints the date stored on the row it read, and names the row". Move the earliest-of-two change out of the benefit column and into a disclosed limitation, and say in one sentence that without per-purchase lots neither merge direction is correct.

findings.heading: CUT 6 — N5a's affected-row-count checks / CUT 2 — N4's live Gemini baseline
findings.quoted_sentence: **Fri 2026-10-02, 18:00.** Fires if cumulative feature hours > 78 and the transfer-route branch is not merged.
findings.what_is_wrong: The trigger is an absolute hour count against a plan that shrinks every time an earlier cut fires: after Cuts 1–5 return 22.25 h the post-cut plan is 72.50 h, so cumulative hours can never exceed 78 and Cut 6 becomes structurally unreachable — the same defect disables Cut 2's "> 58" clause, and it disables them in exactly the scenario (things are going badly, cuts are firing) the triggers exist for.
findings.suggested_fix: Express every hour trigger as a fraction of the CURRENT post-cut plan, not an absolute: "fires if cumulative hours exceed 90% of the remaining plan", and print the recomputed threshold beside each cut so the checkpoint reader can evaluate it aloud.

findings.heading: THE CALENDAR THE CUTS ARE PINNED TO — standing cut checkpoint
findings.quoted_sentence: Standing cut checkpoint: **Saturday 18:00, every week (Sep 20, Sep 27, Oct 4), plus Wednesday 18:00 gates on Sep 30 and Oct 7.** ... No cut is ever discussed off-checkpoint.
findings.what_is_wrong: 2026-09-20, 09-27 and 10-04 are all Sundays (the calendar table three lines above labels them "Sun"), and five of the ten cuts carry triggers on days that are not checkpoints at all — Thu Oct 1 (Cut 5), Fri Oct 2 (Cuts 6 and 7), and Sun Oct 4 at 12:00 (Cuts 8 and 9, four hours before the 18:00 checkpoint) — so the rule the document calls "the part that makes it enforceable" is broken by half its own triggers and gets its own weekday names wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel the weekly checkpoint as Sunday 18:00 (or move it to Sat Sep 19 / Sep 26 / Oct 3), and snap every cut trigger onto a named checkpoint instant; the Oct 7 gate should be deleted, since it falls after the Oct 4 feature freeze and no cut can fire there.

findings.heading: T11 — `success: true` is reported only for writes that happened
findings.quoted_sentence: A 3-item transfer where the `shopping_list_items` DELETE is forced to affect 0 rows (row removed between insert and delete), × 6 forced-failure variants
findings.what_is_wrong: There is no DELETE on `shopping_list_items` in `transfer/route.ts` — the forward path marks items with `.update({ is_checked: true })` at :93–96, and the file's only `.delete()` is at :170 against `user_inventory` in the reverse/undo handler, which never touches `transferred_count` at :112 — so the fixture describes an operation that does not exist and the test as written cannot be built; file 14 line 98 repeats the same conflation and stamps it "both re-confirmed today".
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the fixture around the real mechanism: force the `is_checked` UPDATE at :93–96 to match zero rows (delete the shopping item between the inventory write and the update); assert that the route inspects the affected count rather than only `checkError`. Remove :170 from both files' descriptions of UC20, or describe it separately as a second unchecked write on the undo path.

findings.heading: T3 — The number on screen is the number the system ranked with
findings.quoted_sentence: Today: 1 reference at `:304`; 50/50 render the model's number
findings.what_is_wrong: `grep -c match_score RecipeRecommendationModal.tsx` returns 4 — lines 303, 304, 306 and 307 — and the same table row's own fixture cell already says "today: `RecipeRecommendationModal.tsx:303–304` and `:306–307`", so the baseline contradicts its own row and undercounts the thing the test is supposed to drive to zero by a factor of four.

findings.heading: CUT 1 — N5b, the share-route hardening / THE IRREDUCIBLE CORE (N5a1)
findings.quoted_sentence: it is our first Supabase migration, our first RLS policy and an auth refactor, on a route the receipt does not touch
findings.what_is_wrong: The stated reason for cutting N5b is migration inexperience, yet the irreducible core retains N5a1, whose test (13's T9) explicitly requires "after the new migration, a direct SQL insert of quantity ≤ 0 is rejected by `CHECK (quantity > 0)`", and retains N1b's "seeded local Supabase" — so the capability the document declares too unfamiliar to buy at 8.75 h is assumed available for free inside the core.
findings.suggested_fix: Either drop the inexperience argument from Cut 1 and cut N5b purely on "not on the receipt's path" (which is sufficient on its own), or move the first-migration cost into N1b's 6.0 h explicitly and note that N5a1 reuses it.

findings.heading: THE IRREDUCIBLE CORE — 54.00 h (N5a1)
findings.quoted_sentence: Negatives persist and 0 silently becomes 1, so the receipt would print points for food that is not there. This is the one security item the receipt's honesty is literally made of.
findings.what_is_wrong: Nothing in the scorer as specified (13's T6 enumerates its branches: expired, ≤1 d, ≤3 d, ≤7 d, >7 d, NULL date, not in pantry, duplicate ingredient, 0-ingredient recipe — quantity is not among them) reads quantity at all, so the receipt's honesty is secured by one `quantity > 0` predicate in the pure scorer being written anyway at N2a, not by a 3.0 h write-path fix plus a migration on a route the document elsewhere argues is off the receipt's path.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the quantity floor into N2a as a filter predicate (≈0 h), demote N5a1 to a disclosed-not-fixed finding alongside Cuts 6 and 10, and re-state the core as 51.00 h — or, if the write-path fix is genuinely wanted, justify it on data-integrity grounds rather than on a receipt path it does not sit on.

findings.heading: T5 — Correct one line and the ranking moves (the non-tautological half)
findings.quoted_sentence: Fails if the fraction is **< 0.20** (receipt is decorative: corrections do not reach the ranking) **or > 0.95** (receipt is chaotic: any edit reshuffles everything). Pre-registered; no amount of careful coding guarantees landing inside the band
findings.what_is_wrong: 0.20 and 0.95 have no derivation anywhere in the document — no prior, no pilot, no reference system — so the only non-tautological threshold in the entire M0 evaluation, the one the closing paragraph names as "the only outcome we cannot engineer around", is a model-invented band with two decimal places and the pre-registration ritual is being used to launder it.
findings.suggested_fix: Either derive the band (e.g. from the rank-position distribution of the top flagged item across the ten pantries, computed offline before the scorer is written, and show that computation), or drop the band entirely and pre-register only the direction and the reporting rule: "we report the fraction as it comes out, whatever it is" — which is the stance the closing paragraph already takes and is defensible without an invented number.

findings.heading: U3 — UNTESTABLE as stated — downgrade to a dated citation
findings.quoted_sentence: "All fourteen live products tell you a recipe matches and none tells you why" ... keep the 2026-09-13 archived snapshots in `p1b/evidence/` and cite them with the date, do not re-assert as current
findings.what_is_wrong: Later runs establish that this claim was never true as of that date, not merely un-re-runnable: RecipeFix ships substitution reasoning, Mealie renders "Substituting: {substitute} for {food}" in public shipped source, Remy prints "Using up before they expire: <item> · <qty>", and Cooklist's expiry reminders are confirmed shipping by real user reviews — so dating the citation preserves a false sentence rather than retiring it, and the "Samsung Food returned HTTP 403" justification is stale against the first-party Wayback capture.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the fourteen-products sentence outright rather than downgrading it, and replace the gap statement with the four-way conjunction that actually survives — named item + actual expiry date + nutrient constraint + reason for the substitution, in one auditable correctable object — with the four counter-examples cited by name as the reason the narrower claim is the one being made.

findings.quoted_sentence: | **N2e** Integration and review of the scorer | 2.0 | |
findings.what_is_wrong: In a table whose entire premise is that "Nothing here has a trigger, because nothing here may be cut" and whose third column is headed "Why it cannot go", this row's justification cell is empty — the single clearest evidence that the core is partly what the author kept rather than what cannot be cut.

findings.heading: F0 — BASELINE ROW (do this first)
findings.quoted_sentence: **3 repeats** = 30 live `gemini-2.5-flash` calls (`:217`); archive all 30 raw JSON bodies ... (a) is 0/100 **by construction**
findings.what_is_wrong: 30 calls at `num_recipes=10` return 300 recommendations, not 100, so the denominator in assertion (a) — and in T1's baseline "F0(a): 0/100" and T4's "across 100 recommendations" — is one repeat's worth, while file 14's Cut 2 describes the same artifact as "~100 calls, once"; three different counts of the same run are in circulation.

findings.heading: T8 — The ranking moved behind an authenticated route and stops spending our quota
findings.quoted_sentence: grep finds no `NEXT_PUBLIC_PYTHON_BACKEND_URL` under `web/src/app/dashboard/` ... Today, same harness against FastAPI: **3/3 accepted, 3 Gemini calls, 2 grep hits** (`dashboard/inventory/page.tsx:29` and `:141`
findings.what_is_wrong: That string occurs exactly once in the whole `web/src` tree, at :29; line 141 reads `fetch(\`${BACKEND_URL}/inventory-recommend\`)` and contains no such token — so the baseline is 1, not 2, and the test as literally specified is passed by renaming the constant while leaving the call intact, which is the same source-text-grep-as-security-test pattern already flagged against P1a.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the grep condition with an executed assertion: the call-counting spy records 0 calls when the dashboard page is rendered, plus an AST check that no module under `web/src/app/dashboard/` imports a cross-origin fetch target. Correct the baseline to 1 hit.

findings.heading: T8 — fixture, case (c)
findings.quoted_sentence: (c) valid session for user A naming user B's inventory
findings.what_is_wrong: Today's FastAPI endpoint takes `inventory: List[InventoryItem]` in the request body, so there is no inventory to "name" and no ownership boundary to cross — case (c) is not expressible against the pre-change build, which makes the stated baseline "3/3 accepted" a count of three things only two of which exist.

strongest_things: 13-name-the-test.md — the U1–U5 block, placed first on purpose, that DELETES five benefits outright rather than softening them ('Claims that cannot be tested inside one month are marked UNTESTABLE and deleted from the mission statement, not softened'). Protect it; just fix U3's stale content and U1's stated reason.

13-name-the-test.md — the F0-first design that turns the baseline into a committed archive: 'one prior run against the live gemini-2.5-flash endpoint (30 calls, archived as JSON) supplying the baseline so that no marker ever has to re-run it or hold an API key', paired with the volunteered admission that T1 and T2 'are trivial and today's build does not have them'. Pre-empting the triviality objection in the document's own closing paragraph is exactly right and should not be edited out.

14-cut-list.md — the arithmetic, which closes exactly and independently in two directions: the ten cuts return 8.75+3.5+4+2+4+3.5+2.5+3+6+3.5 = 40.75 h, every running margin figure (14.00 → 17.50 → 21.50 → 23.50 → 27.50 → 31.00 → 33.50 → 36.50 → 42.50 → 46.00) is correct, 94.75 − 40.75 = 54.00 matches the core table's twelve rows summed, and the cut hours re-aggregate to N1 12 + N2 24 + N3 22 + N4 18 + N5a 10 + N5b 8.75 = 94.75. I checked all of it; none of it is off by a single decimal.

14-cut-list.md — the 'The poster must STOP saying: <struck sentence>. Replace with: <exact replacement>' mechanism on all ten cuts. This is what converts a cut list from an intention into an enforceable artifact, and the pairing with 'any cut that fires is executed and its poster sentence deleted in the same sitting' is the strongest process idea in either document. Keep it verbatim.
result.overall:
Neither file is sound as it stands, but they fail in opposite ways and the damage is concentrated in about six places.

14-cut-list.md is arithmetically immaculate and structurally clever — I verified every hour figure, every running margin, and the milestone re-aggregation, and all of it closes exactly. Its problems are argumentative, and one of them is severe: the sentence the irreducible core's poster paragraph is built on — 'grep -c "validate\\|verify\\|check" over the 245-line file returns 0 ... No line of code anywhere recomputes or checks that number' — is true only because grep is case-sensitive. Run it with -i and you get one hit: line 238, a comment reading `# Validate and return`, attached to the Pydantic construction that does validate the model's output. The document explicitly invites a marker to re-run the command. That is the Sketch-mockup failure repeating itself, this time on our own claimed first-hand verification, and it is in the one paragraph the file says 'survives all ten cuts'. The narrower claim available underneath it is actually stronger and fully demonstrable: match_score: int  # 0-100 at :50 carries its range in a comment while num_recipes at :42 on the same model enforces ge=1, le=10 — the field the user reads is the one field the schema declines to constrain.

13-name-the-test.md has the better epistemics (the UNTESTABLE-and-delete block is genuinely admirable) and the worse execution. Its baselines are the assignment's question and the answer is: five of thirteen are predictions wearing the word 'measured' ('measured, expect 4/8', 'expect 0/7', 'expect 6/6', '5/5 would change'), two are arithmetically wrong against the repository I just checked (T3 says 1 match_score reference where there are 4, contradicting its own fixture cell; T8 says 2 grep hits for NEXT_PUBLIC_PYTHON_BACKEND_URL where there is 1), one names a code path that does not exist (T11's 'shopping_list_items DELETE' — the forward path does .update({is_checked:true}) at :93-96, and the file's only .delete() is on user_inventory at :170 in the undo handler), and one — T10's benefit, 'the date that actually disqualifies the food' — is unachievable in a schema that sums quantities with no per-purchase lots, where the proposed 3.5 h fix merely inverts the error. The 0.20–0.95 band in T5, which the closing paragraph correctly identifies as the only outcome the team cannot engineer around, has no derivation of any kind.

The two files also render opposite budget verdicts on the same day: 13 says 'that does not close', 14 opens with 'nothing essential is at risk from the budget'. And the 'irreducible core' is not quite irreducible — N2e's justification cell is literally empty, N5a1's 3.0 h is defended on a receipt path the receipt does not read (a quantity>0 predicate in the pure scorer does the same job for free), N3b spends 2.0 h authenticating a route that Cut 3's own replacement sentence retires, and N5b is cut for migration inexperience while the core quietly assumes a migration and a seeded local Supabase.

Ranked triage if you fix only five things: the grep sentence; the 13-vs-14 budget contradiction; T10's unachievable benefit; the absolute-hour triggers (Cut 2's >58 and Cut 6's >78) that become unreachable as earlier cuts shrink the plan; and the checkpoint calendar, which calls three Sundays 'Saturday' and dates five of ten triggers on days it declares off-limits for discussing cuts.

findings.heading: DISAGREEMENT REGISTER — D10 / §D9-D10 'The IDOR may not exist'
findings.quoted_sentence: The "security tests" are **source-text greps** (`expect(route).toContain('.eq("user_id", user.id)')`), not executed attacks. Neither P1a nor Codex says so.

Backend tests instantiate the actual Pydantic request models and prompt builder, so their accepted inputs are directly confirmed behavior" — and again in `p1a/traceability/final-traceability.md:12` ("`Static contract` ... does not execute the route"), so our flagship methodological reversal accuses our own artifact of a concealment it did not commit, and 03's lede repeats the same charge ("reporting eleven failures without saying so inflates them") while listing ATTACK-RESULTS.md in its own Files-referenced block.

That is still a real finding against Codex and against our summaries, and it survives a marker opening the file.

findings.heading: 4. The three defects that MUST be fixed before any new feature ships
findings.quoted_sentence: **Deliberately not on this list:** D10 (achievement trigger) — service-role write of unvalidated input is a pattern worth fixing, but `user_id` is server-derived, so a user can only pollute their own row; it is a cleanup, not a blocker.

findings.heading: 1. The disagreements, with the evidence — D1 / D2, table row 'Production TS/TSX/PY files in repo (excl. tests, node_modules)'

The single-point-of-failure argument is actually *stronger* against a 192-file codebase, because it removes the 'nobody could learn that' escape hatch. While editing, fix the same table's '530 / 467 → 63' (repo now reports 531 / 64) and '7 code files, **all** under `web/tests/p1a/` or `backend/tests/sihao/p1a/`' — two of them are `p1a/scripts/run_local_model.py` and `run_step7.py`.

findings.heading: D6 / D7 — SAFE is not safe, and the metric is the reason ("What I would put in the mission statement instead")

result.overall:
Neither file is sound as written, and the damage is concentrated in the two paragraphs each one exists to produce: 03's poster boast and 06's methodological reversal.

The worst finding is shared by both. 06's D10 ("Neither P1a nor Codex says so") and 03's lede ("reporting eleven failures without saying so") accuse our own P1a artifact of concealing that the web security tests are source greps. P1a disclosed it twice — in the opening paragraph of ATTACK-RESULTS.md, which 03 lists in its own Files-referenced block, and in final-traceability.md's header. Our flagship reversal is aimed at the wrong target; the real target is that Codex and our own summary tables quoted the counts without carrying the caveat forward, which is a smaller but survivable finding.

Second: both files miss `GET /api/users` — service-role client, no auth, returns every user's id, fullname and email, zero callers. 06 lists the file among the service-role importers, declares that boundary "the security question in this codebase", then checks the two harmless routes and budgets an hour for the twenty-line one that reads the public recipe catalog. 03's "three defects that MUST be fixed" omits it entirely. A later run (p08-mission F5) calls it "worse than the share route" and "the only genuine executed attack" in the whole audit — so the fix for 06's own methodology complaint was sitting one file from where the paragraph stopped.

Third: 06's "9,232-file inherited codebase", load-bearing twice for the single-point-of-failure argument, is 9,075 files of `backend/.venv`. Git tracks 192 non-test TS/TSX/PY files. The argument gets stronger when corrected, which is the good news.

On the assignment's specific question — are the "Status after my check" verdicts backed by checks? Mostly yes, and impressively so: D9 and D10 I reproduced step by step against the schema, the policy, the client construction and the test files. But three verdicts are assertions wearing verdict clothes. D2's "Confirmed error. Also self-contradictory" is manufactured by truncating Codex's sentence at a comma — the dropped half ("but not which current member owns each skill") states the exact distinction D1 accuses Codex of confusing. D1's "rejected it without doing it" is contradicted by the Codex ledger row 06 itself quotes, whose Check column reads "Repository inspection". And D10's "Confirmed" rests on the false premise above.

On estimates: none of the hour figures in either file has a stated basis, and the proof is that the two documents disagree with each other by up to 3.2× on the same fix, written by the same model on the same day (D18 prompt delimiting: 2.5 h in 03, ~8 h in 06). 06's D11 calls Codex's 35 h "a placeholder" and then re-derives exactly 35 h. D7's replacement experiment dismisses a 4-of-5 threshold on Nielsen's "you need 20 users" and then proposes n=10 with invented 60%/20%/45-second thresholds — the one a marker will enjoy most.

Everything here is fixable by editing prose, not by redoing work. The underlying engineering in both files is better than the sentences wrapped around it — which is why the poster paragraph and the disagreement register, the two pieces that will actually be read, are where the effort should go.

## C. Does this read as one document?

No. It reads as **two coherent documents and a cloud of stragglers.**

There is a genuine spine, and it is good: `01 → 05 → 17` (market, corrections, closing the limitations) and `03 → 12 → 14 → 13` (defects, milestones, cuts, tests). Within each of those chains the numbers reconcile to the digit — 12 and 14 agree on all five milestones and on the 94.75 / 40.75 / 54.00 arithmetic, and 13 disagrees with 12 *deliberately and in writing*. That is one author being careful.

The problem is everything that sits between the chains. **09 recommends pivoting away from the product every other file is building, and 16 reports that it recommended the opposite.** The mission statement that is explicitly labelled "the version to print" still carries the 500-case baseline that two later files were written specifically to delete, and specifies a **Python** module while the entire 61-hour test plan is **Jest**. The engineering-evidence file declares three blockers that "MUST be fixed before any new feature ships", and the cut list ships the feature having cut two of them. The five-user comprehension test is killed in 06, 11 and 13 — and then reappears, unflagged, in 15 and 02. The withdrawn Cooklist review, which 05 holds up as the report's proudest self-catch, is still quoted as evidence of demand in 02.

The tell is directional: **every contradiction runs the same way — later runs corrected earlier ones, and the corrections were appended to the files that made them rather than pushed into the files that depend on them.** 17 closed Samsung and Cooklist; 01, 02, 05, 08, 15, 16 and README never heard. 13 re-costed N4; 12 never heard. That is fixable in about two hours: a single "superseded by" pass keyed to runs 4 and 5, plus a decision on four open forks (pivot or not, Python or TypeScript, share route in or out, expired-items excluded or scored-at-zero). Until that pass happens, a marker reading 09 next to 12, or 11b next to 14, finds the disagreement in under a minute — and items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 18 are the ones they will find first.
